title: POCUS and critical care echo
summary: Use focused ultrasound at the bedside as an extension of the examination: obtain the core cardiac views, assess LV and RV function, interpret the IVC and venous congestion carefully, read lung ultrasound patterns (BLUE protocol), run RUSH/eFAST in shock and trauma, and perform two-region compression for DVT.

topics.title: Core cardiac views and LV assessment
topics.summary: Obtain parasternal long and short axis, apical four-chamber and subcostal views. Grade LV function visually (normal, mildly, severely reduced, hyperdynamic) and look for pericardial effusion, gross valve failure and LV size.

steps.title: Phased-array probe
steps.detail: Cardiac preset; marker convention (screen marker on the right in cardiac mode). Patient supine or left lateral.

steps.title: Parasternal long axis
steps.detail: 3rd-4th left intercostal space, marker to right shoulder. LV size and function, mitral and aortic valves, pericardial vs pleural effusion (descending aorta).

steps.title: Parasternal short axis
steps.detail: Rotate 90° clockwise. 'Donut' LV at papillary level: regional wall motion, septal shape (D-sign in RV overload).

steps.title: Apical four-chamber
steps.detail: Apex beat, marker to left. RV:LV size ratio, global function, MAPSE/TAPSE, effusion.

steps.title: Subcostal
steps.detail: Below xiphoid, marker to left, probe flat. Best view in ventilated patients; effusion and RA/RV collapse; then rotate for IVC.

steps.title: LV function
steps.detail: Visual EF: hyperdynamic (cavity obliteration), normal, reduced, severely reduced. E-point septal separation > 7 mm suggests reduced EF.

steps.title: Tamponade
steps.detail: Effusion with RA systolic collapse, RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC; clinical diagnosis with haemodynamic compromise.

tables.title: Five-view focused cardiac scan
rows: Left parasternal, 3rd-4th ICS, marker to right shoulder
LV function, effusion, aortic root, MV/AV
Rotate to long axis, marker cephalad

redFlags.text: Effusion with RV diastolic collapse and hypotension: tamponade → drain.
Severely reduced LV with shock: cardiogenic shock pathway.

pitfalls.text: Calling epicardial fat or a pleural effusion a pericardial effusion (check relation to descending aorta).
Foreshortened apical views underestimating LV size.

pearls.text: Hyperdynamic LV with kissing papillary muscles suggests hypovolaemia or vasodilation.

nodes.text: Normal/hyperdynamic: hypovolaemic or distributive; assess IVC and lungs

consultantNotes.evidence: - **International FoCUS recommendations 2014:** focused cardiac ultrasound is accurate in trained hands for LV dysfunction, RV enlargement, pericardial effusion/tamponade and volume status assessment; it complements but does not replace comprehensive echo.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Portable ultrasound machines are widely available in Indian ICUs; ISCCM and other bodies run POCUS courses. Save images for review and quality assurance.

topics.title: Right ventricle assessment
topics.summary: Compare RV and LV size in the apical four-chamber view, look for septal flattening, measure TAPSE, and interpret signs of acute (thin-walled, McConnell sign) vs chronic (hypertrophied) RV overload.

steps.title: RV:LV ratio
steps.detail: Apical four-chamber: RV basal diameter > 41 mm or RV:LV > 1.0 indicates dilatation.

steps.title: Septum
steps.detail: PSAX D-sign: diastolic flattening = volume overload; systolic flattening = pressure overload.

steps.title: TAPSE
steps.detail: M-mode through lateral tricuspid annulus: < 17 mm = RV dysfunction.

steps.title: Wall thickness
steps.detail: RV free wall > 5 mm suggests chronic pressure overload (pulmonary hypertension); thin dilated RV with McConnell sign (apical sparing) suggests acute PE.

steps.title: Ventilation
steps.detail: High PEEP, hypercapnia and hypoxaemia worsen RV afterload in ARDS (acute cor pulmonale).

redFlags.text: Dilated RV + shock + DVT: treat as massive PE.

pitfalls.text: Foreshortened A4C making the RV look large.

pearls.text: TR peak velocity > 2.8 m/s suggests raised PA pressure; acute PE rarely exceeds ~3.5-4 m/s (RV cannot generate high pressure acutely).

nodes.text: Chronic overload (pulmonary hypertension, chronic lung disease); acute-on-chronic possible
Acute overload: PE, ARDS/high PEEP, RV infarct → module 11

consultantNotes.evidence: - **ASE right-heart guideline 2010:** reference values (RV basal diameter > 42 mm abnormal in that document's tables, TAPSE < 16 mm abnormal; later ASE/EACVI chamber quantification updated to > 41 mm and < 17 mm).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Chronic thromboembolic disease and post-TB lung disease are common causes of chronic RV hypertrophy in India.

quiz.explanation: RV free wall akinesia with apical sparing.

verify.reason: 2010 ASE thresholds (RV > 42 mm, TAPSE < 16 mm) vs 2015 ASE/EACVI (RV > 41 mm, TAPSE < 17 mm). The app uses the 2015 values.

topics.title: IVC and venous congestion (VExUS)
topics.summary: The IVC estimates right atrial pressure in spontaneously breathing patients but predicts fluid responsiveness poorly, especially on the ventilator. A plethoric IVC with abnormal hepatic, portal and intrarenal Doppler (VExUS grade 2-3) signals venous congestion: stop fluids and consider decongestion.

steps.title: IVC
steps.detail: Subcostal long axis, 1-2 cm from RA junction. Spontaneous breathing: < 2.1 cm collapsing > 50% suggests low RAP (~3 mmHg); > 2.1 cm collapsing < 50% suggests high RAP (~15 mmHg).

steps.title: Ventilated
steps.detail: IVC distensibility > 18% may suggest fluid responsiveness in fully ventilated, passive patients with Vt ≥ 8 mL/kg; otherwise unreliable.

steps.title: VExUS
steps.detail: IVC ≥ 2 cm, then hepatic vein (S < D or reversed S), portal vein pulsatility (≥ 30% mild, ≥ 50% severe), intrarenal venous Doppler (biphasic or monophasic).

steps.title: VExUS
steps.detail: 0: IVC < 2 cm. 1: plethoric, normal/mild patterns. 2: one severe pattern. 3: ≥ 2 severe patterns. Grade 3 associated with AKI after cardiac surgery.

steps.title: Congestion
steps.detail: Stop fluids; diuretics or ultrafiltration if perfusion allows; treat RV failure.

redFlags.text: Plethoric IVC with hypotension: tamponade, tension pneumothorax, RV failure or PE.

pitfalls.text: Using a small IVC alone to give large volumes to a ventilated patient.
Raised intra-abdominal pressure compresses the IVC (false 'small IVC').

pearls.text: Portal vein pulsatility is easy to obtain and changes quickly with decongestion.

nodes.text: Low RAP likely; still test fluid responsiveness before fluid
Significant venous congestion: stop fluid, decongest
Plethoric without severe congestion: reassess clinically

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **FoCUS 2014:** IVC size and collapsibility estimate RAP in spontaneously breathing patients.
- **VExUS 2020:** combined Doppler grading predicted AKI after cardiac surgery better than CVP.
consultantNotes.controversies: - VExUS has limited validation outside cardiac surgery and in arrhythmias such as AF.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Doppler-capable ultrasound is needed for VExUS; many Indian ICU machines have it but training is variable.

quiz.stem: IVC 2.4 cm with < 50% collapse in a spontaneously breathing patient suggests RAP of about:

options: Plethoric IVC with ≥ 2 severe Doppler patterns

quiz.stem: IVC is least reliable for fluid decisions in:
options: Ventilated patient with raised abdominal pressure
quiz.explanation: Abdominal pressure and ventilation confound IVC.

topics.title: Lung ultrasound and the BLUE protocol
topics.summary: Lung sliding, A-lines, B-lines, consolidation and effusion answer most bedside questions: pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema vs COPD/asthma, pneumonia, PE and pleural effusion.

steps.title: Probe and points
steps.detail: Linear (pleura) or curvilinear/phased (deeper). BLUE points: upper and lower anterior, and PLAPS point (posterolateral) on each side.

steps.title: Signs
steps.detail: Absent lung sliding + no B-lines + no lung pulse; lung point is specific (diagnostic). Presence of sliding or B-lines rules out pneumothorax at that point.

steps.title: B-lines
steps.detail: ≥ 3 B-lines per intercostal space; bilateral diffuse = pulmonary oedema or ARDS/interstitial disease; focal = pneumonia, contusion.

steps.title: Tissue pattern
steps.detail: Hepatisation, shred sign; dynamic air bronchograms suggest pneumonia rather than resorptive atelectasis.

steps.title: Anechoic space above diaphragm
steps.detail: Spine sign, plankton sign; septations or echogenic fluid suggest exudate/empyema. Estimate volume and mark the site for drainage.

steps.title: Profiles
steps.detail: A-profile + DVT = PE; A-profile + no DVT + PLAPS = pneumonia; A-profile without = COPD/asthma; B-profile = pulmonary oedema; A' profile + lung point = pneumothorax; B' / A/B / C profiles = pneumonia.

tables.title: BLUE protocol profiles
rows: With DVT: PE; with PLAPS: pneumonia; neither: COPD/asthma

redFlags.text: Absent sliding + lung point in a hypotensive ventilated patient: decompress.

pitfalls.text: Absent sliding also occurs with mainstem intubation, apnoea, pleurodesis and large bullae.
B-lines are not specific to pulmonary oedema (also ARDS, fibrosis, pneumonia).

pearls.text: Lung ultrasound beats supine chest X-ray for pneumothorax, effusion and consolidation.

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **BLUE protocol (2008):** 90.5% diagnostic accuracy for the cause of acute respiratory failure.
- **International LUS recommendations 2012:** lung ultrasound is accurate for pneumothorax, interstitial syndrome, consolidation and effusion.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Lung ultrasound is ideal where CT and repeated X-rays are hard to obtain; it was widely used in Indian ICUs during COVID-19.

topics.title: RUSH in shock and eFAST in trauma
topics.summary: RUSH checks the pump (LV, RV, pericardium), the tank (IVC, lungs, peritoneum, pleura) and the pipes (aorta, leg veins) to classify shock in minutes. eFAST looks for free fluid and pneumothorax in trauma.

steps.title: Heart
steps.detail: Effusion/tamponade, LV function, RV size.

steps.title: Volume
steps.detail: IVC, lung B-lines, pleural fluid, peritoneal free fluid (Morison's pouch, splenorenal, pelvis).

steps.title: Vessels
steps.detail: Abdominal aorta (> 3 cm = aneurysm; flap = dissection), femoral and popliteal veins for DVT.

steps.title: eFAST
steps.detail: RUQ, LUQ, pelvis, subxiphoid pericardium, both anterior chests for pneumothorax. Repeat if the patient changes.

steps.title: By pattern
steps.detail: Hypovolaemic, distributive, cardiogenic or obstructive shock (see module 3).

tables.title: RUSH patterns
rows: Normal or small IVC, possible fluid (peritonitis/empyema)

redFlags.text: Positive FAST in a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient: theatre or interventional radiology.

pitfalls.text: A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal or hollow-viscus injury.

pearls.text: Small volumes (< 200 mL) of peritoneal fluid may be missed; repeat scans increase sensitivity.

consultantNotes.evidence:
- **RUSH (2010):** structured approach to shock; subsequent studies show good agreement with final diagnosis.
- **eFAST (2004):** ultrasound was more sensitive than supine chest X-ray for traumatic pneumothorax.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Road traffic injuries are a leading cause of trauma in India; eFAST is a core skill in emergency departments and ICUs (see module 5).

quiz.stem: eFAST adds which assessment to FAST?
Plethoric IVC + RV dilatation + DVT in shock suggests:

topics.title: Two-region compression ultrasound for DVT
topics.summary: Compress the common femoral vein (and saphenofemoral junction) and the popliteal vein with a linear probe. A non-compressible vein means DVT. A negative 2-point scan in a high-probability patient needs repeat at 1 week or a whole-leg scan.

steps.title: Leg
steps.detail: Frog-leg, slight reverse Trendelenburg; linear probe, transverse.

steps.title: Femoral
steps.detail: Common femoral vein from inguinal ligament through saphenofemoral junction to femoral bifurcation; compress every 1-2 cm.

steps.title: Popliteal
steps.detail: Popliteal fossa down to the trifurcation.

steps.title: Compressibility
steps.detail: Full compression = no DVT at that site; incomplete compression = DVT (echogenic thrombus may not be visible).

steps.title: High probability
steps.detail: Repeat in 5-7 days or whole-leg Doppler; combine with D-dimer.

pitfalls.text: Mistaking the artery for the vein (artery is round and pulsatile, does not compress).

pearls.text: Proximal DVT in a patient with shock and RV dilatation strongly supports PE.

nodes.text: No proximal DVT; repeat scan or whole-leg Doppler if high probability

consultantNotes.evidence: - **Bernardi 2008:** serial 2-point compression plus D-dimer was equivalent to whole-leg Doppler for symptomatic DVT.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Intensivist-performed DVT scans are quick and reduce transport for formal Doppler studies.
